title: About
text:
About Design For Impact


Design For Impact is a collaborative scaffold for helping statistical practitioners and domain experts align on purpose, connect analytical choices to stakeholder needs, and communicate evidence in ways that support action.


The project was created by Jett Palmer through graduate research in statistics at California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo. It responds to a practical challenge in statistical collaboration: technically sound analysis does not create impact automatically. Impact also requires alignment, intentionality, and translation.






Developed through research and iteration.



Design For Impact began as an exploration of how statistical collaborators could plan for and evaluate impact more explicitly. The process model and artifact were refined through feedback from statistics students and practitioners working in academia and industry. Their experiences helped clarify the tool’s benefits, limitations, component definitions, and implementation guidance.


The current version is intended to be flexible. It can serve as a shared project document, supplement an existing collaborative workflow, or provide a mental model for practitioners who already use similar habits informally.







About the creator



Jett Palmer is a statistics researcher and consultant whose work focuses on statistical collaboration, organizational problem solving, and translating evidence into action. He created Design For Impact as part of his graduate research at Cal Poly, San Luis Obispo.

title: The Tool
text:
The Tool


Design For Impact turns alignment, intentionality, and translation into a practical process for statistical collaboration.

Download the Tool + Guide

The download includes the blank tool followed by implementation prompts for each component. It is currently provided as a printable PDF.







The five components are designed to be revisited as an engagement develops.








Five components connect purpose, analysis, and action.


Each component supports a different part of the work while keeping the intended impact in view.





Vision — Q1


The long-term goal this collaboration will help advance for the organization or team.


Questions to consider:



If this work were exceptionally successful, what contribution would it make to society or the bottom line?


What purpose, cause, or belief motivates the project?


What long-term outcome will serve as the guiding light?





Impact — Q1


The people this work will serve and the decisions or actions the evidence will enable.


Questions to consider:



Who will be affected by this work beyond the immediate collaborators?


How will stakeholders use the evidence?


Which decisions or actions should the work support?





Partnership — Q1


The expectations and motivations each collaborator brings to a successful working relationship.


Questions to consider:



What does each collaborator hope to gain and contribute?


What are the expectations for scope and timeline?


Are there expectations involving compensation, authorship, or ownership?





Analysis Pathway — Q2


A shared plan for gathering evidence that will enable the intended impact.


Questions to consider:



What do stakeholders seek to understand, compare, explain, or predict?


Which study design, dataset, model, or visualization best meets those needs?


How does the planned analysis connect back to the intended impact?



If the pathway changes substantially, document what was learned in Narrative and begin a new version of the tool.




Narrative — Q3


The concise, evidence-based story of how the analysis contributed to the vision, impact, or partnership.


Questions to consider:



What is the key takeaway?


Who needs to hear it, and how should it be tailored?


How do the findings enable a decision or action?


Which direct or indirect stakeholders should be considered?










A scaffold, not a script.


Use the tool as a shared document between you and your collaborator, or adapt it to your needs.





Use the full artifact


Complete and revise the document collaboratively throughout the engagement.




Integrate selected components


Bring relevant prompts into scoping conversations, intake forms, meeting agendas, statements of work, or project notes.




Use it as a mental model


Apply Vision, Impact, Partnership, Analysis Pathway, and Narrative without requiring collaborators to interact directly with the artifact.




Partial implementation can still improve alignment and intentionality.







Throughout the project


Use the tool as a lightweight record of the thinking that connects one phase of collaboration to the next.





Before kickoff


Review the guide and prepare questions about Vision, Impact, and Partnership. Treat preliminary entries as hypotheses to validate.




During or immediately after kickoff


Establish Q1 with collaborators and confirm that the artifact reflects a shared understanding.




Before substantive analysis


Develop an Analysis Pathway connecting the design, data, methods, and communication products to the intended impact.




During analysis


Use the tool as a pulse-check. Revisit Q1 and Q2 when limitations, findings, or collaborator feedback change the project. Preserve prior versions after substantive changes.




Before closeout


Draft a Narrative connecting the evidence to the stakeholders, decisions, or actions identified in Q1. Tailor separate Narratives when audiences have different needs.




During and after closeout


Validate the Narrative with collaborators and incorporate it into presentations, reports, executive summaries, handoff materials, or project records.









Ways to adapt it


Implementation can be as formal or lightweight as an engagement calls for.




Asking more vision- and impact-oriented questions during scoping


Incorporating components into an intake form or statement of work


Documenting tried-and-revised Analysis Pathways


Revisiting the tool during standing client check-ins


Drafting a one- or two-sentence impact Narrative before closeout


Using the structure privately in meeting notes when a shared artifact is impractical



Not every project needs every approach.








Teaching Design For Impact


Instructor materials are in development, including presentation materials and a complete lesson or workshop plan. In the meantime, instructors may use the Tool + Guide and completed examples to introduce impact-centered statistical collaboration.

title: Design For Impact
text:
Design For Impact


A collaborative scaffold for maximizing and communicating impact in statistical collaboration.


Download the Tool + Guide Learn More







A fillable guide for planning, revisiting, and communicating impact throughout a statistical engagement.







Impact doesn’t happen automatically—it requires alignment, intentionality, and translation.







From evidence to action.


Design For Impact builds on the Q1Q2Q3 framework developed by Vance and colleagues, which moves from qualitative context gathering, through quantitative analysis, to qualitative interpretation.





Q1


Qualitative



→



Q2


Quantitative



→



Q3


Qualitative






Alignment


Establish the project’s broader vision, intended impact, and expectations for the partnership.




Intentionality


Choose the design, dataset, analytical approach, and communication products that enable the intended impact.




Translation


Develop an audience-specific, evidence-based narrative connecting the findings to the stakeholders, decisions, or actions identified in Q1.





The tool turns these principles into five practical components.

title: Examples
text:
Design For Impact in action.


These fictitious examples show how the same five components can support collaborations with different goals, stakeholders, and definitions of impact. They are illustrations, not templates: each project should adapt the tool to its own context.

Review the Tool and Implementation Guide →






Marketing Campaign Optimization


A statistical practitioner is helping a marketing team identify customer segments for an upcoming campaign and decide how to allocate its budget.





Vision — Q1


Maximize customer engagement and lifetime value through more personalized marketing strategies.




Impact — Q1


Help the marketing team allocate its budget across customer segments to maximize conversion.




Partnership — Q1


Deliver within two weeks, before the next campaign-planning cycle begins.




Analysis Pathway — Q2


Fit a logistic model to estimate conversion probability across customer segments, accompanied by interpretable visualizations that guide budgetary decisions.




Narrative — Q3


The model identified a customer segment with a significantly higher likelihood of conversion. Marketing shifted its budget toward this segment, increasing overall conversion from 8% to 14% and generating $86,000 in additional revenue.




What this illustrates: The business goal, stakeholder decision, project timeline, analysis, and final result remain connected throughout the engagement.







Environmental Attitudes and Behavior


Environmental psychology researchers and a statistical collaborator are studying why environmental concern does not always translate into sustainable behavior.





Project


Environmental concern and sustainable behavior




Collaborators


Environmental psychology researchers and statistical collaborator




Engagement period


2026 academic year




Version


1






Vision — Q1


Advance understanding of why environmental concern does not always translate into sustainable behavior.




Impact — Q1


Determine whether the attitude-behavior gap depends on context, measurement, and access to sustainable choices, helping researchers design future studies and more effective interventions.




Partnership — Q1


All collaborators will appear as co-authors on a paper targeting environmental psychology journals. The team agrees that null or mixed findings remain valuable and will still be submitted for publication.




Analysis Pathway — Q2


Use multilevel regression to determine how the relationship between environmental concern and behavior varies by context, measurement approach, and access to sustainable choices. Compare results across measures and settings to help researchers identify priorities for future studies and promising targets for behavioral interventions.




Narrative — Q3


Environmental concern was more strongly associated with self-reported than observed behavior, particularly when sustainable alternatives were difficult to access. Researchers can prioritize access and measurement in their next study and design interventions that reduce practical barriers rather than focusing only on attitudes.




What this illustrates: Academic impact may involve contributions to a body of knowledge, decisions about what to study next, and the design of future interventions rather than an immediate organizational outcome.
